conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m Dr. Miller, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to check in on how you’re feeling now that your baby has arrived, and to make sure you’re getting any support you might need.

We’ll be using a short, well-studied questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**. It’s just 10 questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past week. There are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you. Everything you share stays confidential within our care team, and we’ll take it at your pace in a safe, judgment-free space.

When you’re ready, I’ll ask the first question:

Over the past seven days, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?
I can still laugh sometimes, but it’s definitely harder than it used to be. Things that would normally make me chuckle feel kind of distant or not worth the effort.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes I can laugh a little, but it doesn’t come as easily as before—mostly I feel too tired or worried about the baby to really find things funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Not really. I mean, I still want to enjoy things, but when I think about doing stuff I used to like—coffee with friends, even just a walk—it feels more like a chore than something to look forward to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times. If the baby won’t settle or I can’t get her to nap, I catch myself thinking I must be doing something wrong or that a “better mom” would figure it out faster. It’s not constant, but it pops in more than I’d like.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I do feel anxious, but it’s usually about the baby—like whether she’s breathing okay at night or if I’m feeding her enough. It’s not totally “no reason,” but the worry feels bigger than it probably should.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times, yeah. I’ll be sitting there, everything looks fine, and suddenly my heart races like something awful is about to happen. It passes pretty quickly, but it leaves me feeling shaky and on-edge.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. Between feedings, diapers, and trying to grab a shower, it feels like I’m always one step behind. I manage, but by evening I’m exhausted and counting the minutes until my partner gets home so I can hand her off.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m that unhappy—more just tense and overtired. I lie down and my mind keeps running through the day, worrying I forgot something or that she’ll wake up any minute. Takes me a while to drift off, and then I’m up again when she cries.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the time—like little waves that come and go. It’s not all day, but when they hit, everything feels heavier and I just want to sit in the nursery with the lights low until it passes.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I’ve teared up once or twice this week—usually when I’m really worn out—but I haven’t had those big, can’t-stop crying spells. Mostly I just feel kind of numb and exhausted rather than weepy.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’m tired and overwhelmed, but I would never want to hurt myself. My baby needs me, and I want to be here for her.

You've shared that the last week has felt heavy-laughter and excitement come rarely, replaced by near-constant worry about your baby and a sense that each day is "getting on top of me" (<quote>most days, yeah</quote>). Sadness washes over you in waves, and when the baby won't settle you quickly blame yourself (<quote>a better mom would figure it out faster</quote>). Although you're meeting her needs, the joy feels distant, sleep is hard to find, and brief surges of panic leave you shaky. You showed courage in revealing these feelings and strength in firmly stating you would never harm yourself; your baby and your own hope keep you moving forward.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 16, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only occasional laughter with clear reduction from baseline due to fatigue and worry, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient clearly reports diminished enjoyment and anticipatory pleasure, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame recurring "more than I'd like" but not constant, aligning with "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurrent, disproportionate worry about baby's safety/feeding, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden episodes of panic with physical symptoms (heart racing, shaky, on-edge) that occur a couple of times, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily overwhelm and needing rescue from partner, fitting "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>She describes recurrent waves of sadness and heaviness that interrupt her day, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 16 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale places you above the 14-point cut-off indicating probable major <med>depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Endorsement of <sym>anhedonia</sym>, frequent <sym>sadness</sym>, self-blame, and multiple anxiety symptoms aligns with DSM-5 criteria (≥5 symptoms for ≥2 weeks causing impairment). Item 10 self-harm score is 0, removing immediate safety concern but not diminishing clinical urgency. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to confirm diagnosis and discuss treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based therapies such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med> or <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> for postpartum depression
3. Discuss possible <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding if symptoms remain moderate-to-severe
4. Schedule within 48 h follow-up call to review mood, coping, and any new thoughts of self-harm
5. Begin gentle daily routine: 20-min rest when baby sleeps, balanced meals, and brief outdoor walk to improve <sym>sleep</sym> and <sym>energy</sym>
6. Share Edinburgh results with a trusted support person and keep crisis numbers handy (<med>National Maternal Mental Health Hotline</med> 1-833-943-5746)
7. Plan re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress after interventions
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother (baby ~ weeks old)  
Instrument: Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) – self-report  
Date: _____________

Symptoms / concerns endorsed  
• Anhedonia: diminished ability to laugh, reduced anticipatory pleasure  
• Low mood: intermittent sadness, “waves” of feeling heavy  
• Mild tearfulness (no prolonged crying spells)  
• Excessive guilt / self-blame re infant care  
• Persistent, baby-focused worries; occasional abrupt panic-like surges (no clear trigger)  
• Subjective feeling of “getting on top of me” most days; end-of-day exhaustion  
• Sleep-onset difficulty linked to intrusive worries, not mood-congruent insomnia  
• Denies any self-harm ideation (EPDS Q10 = 0)

Pattern  
Mild-to-moderate depressive and anxiety symptoms present; functioning impaired but able to meet infant’s basic needs. No safety red flags.

Screening significance  
Elevated scores consistent with possible minor-moderate postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety; does not meet threshold for severe episode or psychosis. Continue monitoring, consider formal assessment (PHQ-9, GAD-7) and psycho-education; rule-out thyroid / anemia.
